text: Hey, I’m Marcus. I grew up on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, near the Choptank River, and last summer I led walking tours on the same roads Harriet Tubman knew as a girl. This year I’m writing my first research paper about her, so we’re learning together. Today you’ll read Chapter 1. Here’s the question: what does one ordinary day tell us about Harriet’s life, and about what she dreams of?

Freedom Watch. On my tours, I’d stop people at the edge of a marsh and ask them to just look for one minute. Most people noticed more in that minute than on the whole walk. Harriet can’t leave the house where she works, but she can look. Watch what she sees through the window, and what it makes her wonder. Sometimes freedom starts that small.

Chapter 1 opens on a spring day that’s beautiful outside and full of work inside. Keep track of what Harriet does, what she eats, and where her eyes go when nobody is watching her. Near the end, something goes badly wrong. Notice who comes looking for her, and the question she asks him. I underlined that question in my own copy.

Hey, it’s Marcus. Chapter 1 ended with Harriet in a peck of trouble, and Chapter 2 is named for it. When I started my research, I thought her story would begin with an escape. It doesn’t. It begins with a girl who won’t give in, even in small ways. Today’s question: what kind of trouble is Harriet in, and what does it tell us about her?

Today’s Freedom Watch is about small rebellions. Harriet can’t escape, and she can’t fight back. But there’s one thing she will not do, no matter who asks her, not even her own mother. Watch for it. This chapter has a hard part in it, so take it slowly. Then ask yourself: is saying no quietly still a kind of freedom? And what does it cost her?

Chapter 2 starts in the cabin where Harriet’s family lives. Pay attention to the cabin itself: the fireplace, the beds, and one thing her mother made by hand. Then listen to what her mother and her father each say about smiling. They don’t agree. Watch where Harriet stands. That handmade thing shows up in your word game, too.

Hey, it’s Marcus. Harriet never went to school, not for a single day. So how did she learn so much? That’s what Chapter 3 is about. Sterling calls it School Days, and I think she means it with a little bit of a smile. Keep a tally of every teacher Harriet has. Today’s question: what does school mean for an enslaved child in Maryland?

Freedom Watch: learning what you’re not supposed to know. In Harriet’s time, the law tried to keep enslaved people from learning to read. But learning found other ways in: stories, songs, and news passed from cabin to cabin. On my tours, people were always surprised how fast news traveled without a single phone. Watch how much Harriet learns without a book.

There’s no schoolhouse in Chapter 3, but there are teachers everywhere. Notice the old man who can read, and what he reads aloud. Notice the songs, and what they might really mean. Then notice the walks in the woods near the end. I’ve walked woods like those. What is Harriet learning there that no book could teach her?

Hey, it’s Marcus. Harriet is fifteen now, and stronger than most of the grown men she works beside. In Chapter 4 she meets someone who has already run away twice, and she starts hearing about trains, the real kind and another kind. Today’s question: what does a train mean to Harriet? Here’s a hint: it isn’t only about riding.

Freedom Watch: hearing the whistle. Before anyone can go somewhere new, they have to hear that it’s there. Listen for the stories Harriet hears in this chapter, and who tells them. Notice what happens inside her while she listens, even though she doesn’t say a word. Then think about a story you once heard that changed what you thought was possible.

In Chapter 4, Harriet meets Jim, who has already tried to run away twice. Listen to his stories about the steam train, and about another railroad with very unusual conductors. Watch for the song the workers sing in the barn. The chapter ends suddenly, with a hard choice and a frightening moment. Take a breath there, and watch what Harriet decides.
